podcast.title: Ancestor of Country Music
podcast.body: Hillbilly music is identified as an ancestor of country music, formed by mixing stories told in song, rhythmic influences, and instruments like the banjo, which originated from Africa. "Stories were told in song mix in the rhythmic influences and instruments like the banjo which came from Africa and you have hillbilly music which is an ancestor of country."

srcs.episode: Ep. 23 - Women of Country Music in the 70s

podcast.title: BMI's Role
podcast.body: BMI, established as a rival to ASCAP, focused on licensing "low-class music," which included hillbilly music. The ASCAP Boycott of 1941 led to a year where hillbilly music was one of the few genres widely playable on radio, giving it free publicity and a greatly expanded audience, especially when artists incorporated the boogie style. "BMI dealt with only the low-class music, the blues, and country songs, and gospel songs, and hillbilly music, and boogie."

podcast.title: Early Radio Exposure (1940s)
podcast.body: Hillbilly music, along with country, folk, and R&B, saw increased exposure on radio in the 1940s as stations turned to music from performers outside of the ASCAP collective due to a format war. "This meant more country and folk and hillbilly and R&B were heard on the radio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Increased Radio Exposure (WWII Era)
podcast.body: During World War II, changes in radio programming, including local stations being allowed local programming after 7 pm and the cost-effectiveness of playing records, created space for "hillbilly" records. This allowed listeners to hear the genre, contributing to a broader dissemination of diverse musical styles across the American airwaves. "But it also made room for country, western, hillbilly, and R&B records. People started to hear other genres on the radio for the very very first time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: More Granular Classification
podcast.body: Hillbilly music was one of the more granular genre classifications available in 1955, illustrating that even during a period of broad musical categorization, there were efforts to define more specific styles. "You could slice certain genres into thinner slices to include big band, Dixie Land, Scott, Hillbilly, and Jazz, gospel, Broadway show music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Predecessor to Country Music
podcast.body: In the World War I era, what is now known as country music was referred to as Hillbilly music. During this period, black and white musicians frequently played together and mutually influenced each other, indicating the genre's integrated origins. "What we now call country was Hillbilly music in the World War I era and black and white musicians played together and influenced each other."

podcast.title: Roots Music Category
podcast.body: Hillbilly music is identified as a type of roots music that, along with bluegrass, requires an environment where it can be heard and supported. "However, there does need to be space made for all types of roots music, including blue grass and hillbilly music."
